subtype: Smirk and sneer as social judgement [Interpreting]
passage: Vaibhav's diary, Tuesday night. Indu smirked at me today when Sir called me to the board and I dropped the chalk. I was sure she was laughing at me, and I was so angry I didn't talk to her at lunch. But then Sir asked HER a question and she smirked again, only this time she was biting her lip and fiddling with her pencil box. Maybe that's just what her face does when she's nervous? I don't know. I'll ask her tomorrow instead of guessing. I don't want to be unfair to her 😅

qa.q: What did Vaibhav drop at the board?
qa.a: He dropped the chalk.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav first think Indu's smirk meant, and what made him doubt it?
qa.a: He first thought she was laughing at him. When she smirked again while biting her lip and fiddling with her pencil box, he wondered whether it is just her nervous face.

qa.q: What would you advise Vaibhav to do?
qa.a: Ask her kindly tomorrow instead of guessing, as he plans, and maybe say what he felt when he dropped the chalk.

qa.q: How might Indu feel if she knew Vaibhav ignored her at lunch?
qa.a: Probably confused or hurt. If she was only nervous, she had no idea her face looked mocking.

grounding: A child reads a smirk as mockery but notices it may be nervousness, and decides to ask.

subtype: Smirk and sneer as social judgement [Interpreting]
passage:
At the kasba school, Harish stumbled on a word while reading aloud from the Hindi reader. In the next row Ojas curled one side of his mouth. Harish's face burned. He thinks he's better than me, he thought, and stopped reading until Master ji nodded for him to go on.
After the bell Harish swallowed and asked, “Were you laughing at me?”
Ojas blinked. “No! I'm next, and my stomach is like a tight rope. My mouth goes funny when I'm scared.”
“Oh.” Harish let out a long breath.

qa.q: Where was Ojas sitting?
qa.a: Ojas was sitting in the next row.

qa.q: What was Harish feeling when he stopped reading, and what else might explain Ojas's look?
qa.a: Hurt and embarrassed, since his face burned and he assumed Ojas thought he was better. The look turned out to be nerves, so his assumption was one possible reading, not the only one.

qa.q: What did Harish do that worked better than assuming an insult?
qa.a: He asked Ojas directly after the bell, and learned that Ojas was nervous about his own turn.

qa.q: What was it like for Ojas to be asked?
qa.a: He was probably surprised that his nervous face looked like mockery, and glad to explain that he was scared, not scornful. 🙂

grounding: A smirk is read as mockery, but asking shows it was nervousness.

subtype: Smirk and sneer as social judgement [Interpreting]
passage: Ivan's shot went wide of the goal, and as he trudged back across the Prague schoolyard he saw Tomas, arms folded, one corner of his mouth pulled up. Heat rushed into Ivan's face. So Tomas thinks I'm useless. He almost said something sharp. Then he noticed Tomas was next in line, bouncing on his heels, picking at his sleeve. When Tomas's own shot hit the post, the same crooked smirk appeared, aimed at no one. At the water tap Ivan asked, “Were you laughing at my miss?” Tomas looked startled. “What? No. My face does that when I'm nervous.”

qa.q: Where did Tomas's own shot land?
qa.a: Tomas's shot hit the post.

qa.q: What was Ivan feeling when he first saw the smirk?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and angry, thinking Tomas saw him as useless; the heat in his face shows the sting.

qa.q: What helped Ivan avoid an unfair quarrel?
qa.a: He watched more context, noticing Tomas's nerves and the same smirk after his own miss, and then asked directly.

qa.q: How might Tomas feel on hearing he looked like he was laughing?
qa.a: Tomas might feel surprised and a bit embarrassed that his nervous face was read as mockery.

grounding: Shows a child reading a classmate's smirk as mockery, then watching the context and asking, and finding it was nervousness.

subtype: Smirk and sneer as social judgement [Interpreting]
passage: In the school hall on science-fair day, Tushar's volcano gave one sad fizz and stopped. Across the table, Sabina's upper lip curled and she glanced at her own model. Tushar's ears went hot. Of course. She thinks hers is miles better. He wanted to say something mean. Instead he waited. When the judge reached Sabina, her hands shook so much she spilled the baking soda. After the judge moved on, Tushar muttered, “You made a face at mine.” Sabina winced. “Sorry. I was thinking, if yours fizzled, mine will too.”

qa.q: What happened when the judge reached Sabina?
qa.a: Her hands shook so much she spilled the baking soda.

qa.q: Why did Tushar's ears go hot?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and stung, reading Sabina's curled lip as her thinking her model was much better.

qa.q: What went right because Tushar waited?
qa.a: He saw Sabina's shaking hands and then asked, which showed her face came from worry, not scorn, and stopped him saying something mean.

qa.q: What was the science fair like for Sabina?
qa.a: She was nervous that her model would fail too, and her face was about her own fear rather than judging Tushar.

grounding: Shows a child reading a sneer as superiority, then seeing more context and asking, and learning it came from nerves.

subtype: Smirk and sneer as social judgement [Interpreting]
passage: I'm Rafiq, and I sit behind Samir in Class 5. On Monday the new boy, Kenji, smirked when Samir read his poem aloud. Samir's neck went red. At break he told me, “Did you see? He thinks my poem's rubbish.” I didn't know. I'd seen Kenji smirk at the fan and the blackboard too. Samir didn't shout, though. He watched Kenji for two days. On Wednesday he asked him straight out, at the tap. I couldn't hear the answer, but Samir came back shrugging. “He says he smiles like that when he's lost.” Now they share a bench.

qa.q: In which class does Rafiq sit behind Samir?
qa.a: Rafiq sits behind Samir in Class 5.

qa.q: What was Samir feeling when his neck went red?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and hurt, believing Kenji thought his poem was rubbish.

qa.q: Which of Samir's choices worked, and why?
qa.a: Watching for two days and then asking Kenji directly worked, because it showed the smirk came from feeling lost, not from mockery.

qa.q: How does Rafiq read Kenji's smirk?
qa.a: Rafiq isn't sure, having seen Kenji smirk at the fan and the blackboard too, so the look seemed less aimed at Samir.

grounding: Shows a child reading a new classmate's smirk as mockery, then watching and asking instead of assuming an insult.

subtype: Smirk and sneer as social judgement [Interpreting]
passage:
Monday: When Jahnavi read her poem about her grandmother's goats aloud, she caught Afreen smirking in the second row, one corner of her mouth pulled up. Jahnavi's cheeks burned. She's laughing at me. She didn't speak to Afreen all day.

Wednesday: The teacher called Afreen to solve a sum on the board. Jahnavi watched her walk up. There it was again, the same lopsided smirk, while Afreen's chalk hand shook and she got the sum wrong.

Friday: At the water tap, Jahnavi asked straight out, "Why did you smirk at my poem?"

Afreen went red. "Did I? I do that face when I'm nervous. I was next to read."

Jahnavi thought about the chalk and the shaking hand.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi's poem about?
qa.a: Her grandmother's goats.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi feel when she first saw Afreen's smirk on Monday?
qa.a: She felt hurt and embarrassed, sure she was being mocked, which is why her cheeks burned and she avoided Afreen all day.

qa.q: Which choice helped Jahnavi understand the smirk, and why?
qa.a: Watching Afreen in another moment and then asking directly; the shaking hand and Afreen's answer showed the look could mean nerves, not an insult.

qa.q: What is it like for Afreen to have a nervous face that looks like a smirk?
qa.a: Afreen may not even know the face shows, so she can be misread as rude and lose friends without meaning anything unkind.

grounding: It shows a school-age child reading a classmate's smirk as mockery, then watching more and asking, and finding it was nervousness.
